Osijek Donji Grad Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Osijek, Croatia

Not demolished. Osijek, Slavonia's largest economic center on the Drava River, grew from Roman-era Mursa through Ottoman destruction (1526) and 160 years of Turkish rule before Austrian development split it into Gornji grad, Donji grad, and the Tvrđa fortress district, unified in 1809. Jews first settled at the end of the 17th century, gaining official settlement rights in Donji grad by 1746; an organized community formed around 160 families by 1847-49. Two separate congregations existed - Gornji grad (larger, with an 1869 synagogue by architect Theodor Stern) and Donji grad (a 1903 neo-Romanesque/neo-Moorish building). By the 1880s-90s, Osijek held Croatia's largest Jewish community, reaching 2,370 by 1910, including notable leader Rabbi Samuel Spitzer and his son Hugo, a pioneering Yugoslav Zionist. Croatian nationalists destroyed the Gornji grad synagogue in 1941 and extorted 20 million dinars from the community before deporting all of Osijek's Jews in June 1942 to Auschwitz and Jasenovac, where none survived. Postwar, about 220 Jews had re-established the community by 1968. This Donji grad cemetery, established in 1860, holds tombstones from 1855 to 1959; its early-1900s chapel, damaged in the 1990s Croatian War, has since been repaired.
